\begin{abstract}
Uncoordinated electric-vehicle (EV) charging raises the energy cost of
distribution feeders and pushes evening voltages below the service-voltage
floor. Pricing, dispatch and voltage regulation act on timescales of hours,
minutes and seconds, yet most learning-based coordinators use one decision
interval. We propose a three-level nested controller. Level~1 (proximal policy
optimization) sets an hourly retail price corridor. Level~2, a deep
deterministic policy gradient agent shared by the aggregators, dispatches
every \SI{15}{min} as a learned residual on a deadline-aware cheapest-slot plan,
and least-laxity-first allocation makes every dispatch feasible for charger
and transformer limits by construction. Level~3 is non-parametric: it models
drivers' price acceptance and, every \SI{60}{s}, corrects voltage with charger
reactive power bounded by the inverter apparent-power rating, falling back to
curtailment only when that headroom is exhausted. We evaluate on the IEEE 33-
and 69-bus feeders with AC power flow, real day-ahead prices, household loads
and charging sessions, \GEvalDays{} held-out days and \GTrainSeeds{} training
seeds. At \GPenSThree\% EV penetration the controller cuts energy cost by
\GSavingNestedUncSThree\% relative to uncoordinated charging with no voltage
violations% claim: nested_zero_viol_nominal
\ (uncoordinated: \GUncoordinatedSThreeViol\% of steps) and is the cheapest
learned controller at every penetration level.% claim: nested_cheapest_learned_main
\ At nominal load it costs \GGapNestedPaSThree\% more than a price-aware
heuristic that executes the same plan per vehicle;% claim: pa_cheaper_than_nested_all_main
\ when the feeder is stressed beyond its reactive capacity, it curtails
\GReductionCurtNestedPaSSeven\% less energy% claim: nested_less_curtailment_than_pa_S7
\ and leaves \GReductionUnmetNestedPaSSeven\% less undelivered.% claim: nested_less_unmet_than_pa_S7
\ Attached to the baselines, Level~3 removes their violations up to
\GPenSFive\% penetration when load forecasts are accurate.% claim: l3_zero_viol_rules_nominal
% claim: l3_zero_viol_learned_nominal
\end{abstract}

\begin{IEEEkeywords}
Deep reinforcement learning, distribution networks, electric vehicle charging,
multi-timescale control, reactive power, residual policy learning, voltage
regulation.
\end{IEEEkeywords}

\section{Introduction}
\IEEEPARstart{G}{lobal} electric-car sales exceeded 17 million in 2024 and are
expected to pass 20 million in 2025~\cite{iea2025}. Residential charging
concentrates in the evening, when drivers return home and household demand is
already at its peak. On weak radial feeders this added load depresses
end-of-line voltages toward and below the $0.95\pu$ lower limit of the
ANSI C84.1 service range~\cite{ansi_c84,clement2010,stiasny2021}, and it buys
energy in the most expensive hours of the day-ahead market. Coordinated
charging can avoid both, because most vehicles stay plugged in far longer than
they need to charge.

Existing coordinators fall into three families. \emph{Optimization-based}
schedulers~\cite{clement2010,ortegavazquez2014} reach good schedules when the
model and the forecasts are accurate, but they need vehicle-level information
over the whole horizon and a network model, and they are usually solved on a
single decision interval. \emph{Decentralized} schemes such as time-of-use
(TOU) tariffs, game-theoretic demand response and priority
rules~\cite{mohsenian2010,ma2013,xu2016priority} scale well but cannot see the
network. \emph{Deep reinforcement learning} (DRL)~\cite{wan2019,zhang2020cddpg,jin2020,dasilva2020,qian2021,park2022,shibl2023,tuchnitz2021,orfanoudakis2025}
learns from data, but most agents are flat: one policy acts at one rate and
voltage limits enter as reward penalties, which give no guarantee.

The underlying problem is a timescale mismatch. Wholesale prices change every
hour, aggregators re-dispatch every few minutes, and voltages respond within
seconds. \emph{Nested learning}~\cite{behrouz2025} views a learning system as a
set of interconnected optimization problems, each updated at its own
frequency. We use it as a design principle: one level per timescale, with
set points passed down and measurements passed up.

This paper makes four contributions.
\begin{enumerate}
\item \textbf{A three-level nested controller} (Section~\ref{sec:method}) that
matches each level to its timescale: an hourly PPO price-corridor policy, a
\SI{15}{min} DDPG dispatch policy shared by all aggregators, and a
non-parametric layer that resolves price acceptance every \SI{15}{min} and
voltage every \SI{60}{s}.
\item \textbf{Plan-residual dispatch with feasibility by construction.} Level~2
learns a correction to a deadline-aware cheapest-slot plan (residual policy
learning~\cite{silver2018residual,johannink2019residual}), so training starts
from a sound schedule instead of from scratch. Least-laxity-first
allocation~\cite{xu2016priority} with a deadline guard maps the aggregate set
point to per-vehicle rates that satisfy charger and transformer limits exactly.
\item \textbf{Inverter-rating-based reactive correction.} Level~3 bounds each
charger's reactive power by $\Qmax_i=\sqrt{S_i^2-P_i^2}$~\cite{leemput2015}, so
curtailing active power never removes reactive headroom. A
measured-sensitivity Newton step closes the voltage gap, and curtailment is
used only when headroom is exhausted. The layer is independent of the policy
above it, and we evaluate it on every baseline as well.
\item \textbf{A reproducible, paired evaluation} (Sections~\ref{sec:system}
and~\ref{sec:setup}) with AC power flow on two IEEE feeders; real ENTSO-E
prices~\cite{hirth2018}, Pecan Street household loads~\cite{pecanstreet} and
ACN-Data sessions~\cite{lee2019acn}; \GEvalDays{} held-out days; three training
seeds; and eight baselines, including a perfect-foresight model-predictive
LP-OPF, PPO-Lagrangian, CPO and a goal-conditioned hierarchical agent. One
command regenerates every number, table and figure in this paper from the
public code.
\end{enumerate}

\section{Related Work}
\label{sec:related}
\emph{Optimization.} Clement-Nyns \emph{et al.}~\cite{clement2010} schedule
plug-in vehicles with quadratic and dynamic programming to limit losses and
voltage deviations, and Ortega-Vazquez~\cite{ortegavazquez2014} adds battery
degradation and price uncertainty at household level. Such schedulers need
forecasts of arrivals, departures and energy needs; we include a
model-predictive LP-OPF with \emph{perfect} foresight as a strong reference.

\emph{Decentralized coordination.} Mohsenian-Rad \emph{et
al.}~\cite{mohsenian2010} formulate demand-side management as a game, and Ma
\emph{et al.}~\cite{ma2013} show that decentralized charging control can fill
the overnight valley. Xu \emph{et al.}~\cite{xu2016priority} show that
schedules can be improved by giving priority to vehicles with less laxity and
longer remaining charging time; our allocation layer follows this principle in
its least-laxity-first form.

\emph{Learning-based charging.} Wan \emph{et al.}~\cite{wan2019} learn
real-time charging with deep Q-learning and price features; Zhang \emph{et
al.}~\cite{zhang2020cddpg} use DDPG; Jin and Xu~\cite{jin2020} exploit the
structure of optimal policies in a distribution network; da Silva \emph{et
al.}~\cite{dasilva2020}, Park and Moon~\cite{park2022} and Qian \emph{et
al.}~\cite{qian2021} study multi-agent and navigation settings; Shibl \emph{et
al.}~\cite{shibl2023} add vehicle-to-grid operation and degradation; Tuchnitz
\emph{et al.}~\cite{tuchnitz2021} control a fleet; and Orfanoudakis \emph{et
al.}~\cite{orfanoudakis2025} scale RL with graph neural networks. Reviews
cover the wider landscape~\cite{fescioglu2023}. EV2Gym~\cite{orfanoudakis2025ev2gym}
and SustainGym~\cite{yeh2023sustaingym} provide simulation benchmarks and,
for this study, the bundled open data. Saner \emph{et
al.}~\cite{saner2022} propose a cooperative hierarchical multi-agent system for
several stations, and Ye \emph{et al.}~\cite{ye2022local} use multi-agent DRL
for local energy markets. Hierarchical RL in general is surveyed
in~\cite{pateria2021}.

\emph{Safe RL and voltage control.} Constrained policy optimization
(CPO)~\cite{achiam2017} and Lagrangian methods treat safety as an expected-cost
constraint; reviews of their use in power systems
are~\cite{su2025review,yu2024safereview}. Safety-constrained DRL has been
applied to Volt-VAR control~\cite{wang2020voltvar,gao2022modelaug}, active
distribution networks~\cite{kou2020}, real-time voltage control with stability
guarantees~\cite{shi2022stability} and multi-agent active voltage
control~\cite{wang2024safemarl}. Multi-agent DRL also coordinates Volt-VAR
devices~\cite{gao2021consensus} and active and reactive power~\cite{hu2022voltage},
and physics-informed graph representations make voltage control robust to bad
measurements~\cite{cao2024pignn}, in the spirit of physics-informed
learning~\cite{raissi2019pinn}. Reactive support from EV chargers has been
studied in~\cite{leemput2015,singh2013,mattos2024} and combined with
active-power control in~\cite{wang2023coord,hu2021dmpc};
inverter reactive capability is standardized for distributed energy resources
in IEEE Std 1547-2018~\cite{ieee1547}.

\emph{Positioning.} Table~\ref{tab:positioning} summarizes the gap. Flat and
safe RL learn one policy at one rate and handle voltage through rewards or
expected-cost constraints; optimization handles voltage through a linearized
model and needs forecasts of all vehicles; hierarchical RL learns several rates
but still learns safety. Our controller separates the timescales, keeps
feasibility out of the learning problem, corrects voltage with physics on the
measured state, and needs only the day-ahead prices and the states of the
plugged-in vehicles.

\section{System Model}
\label{sec:system}

\subsection{Feeder and power flow}
We use the IEEE 33-bus~\cite{baran1989} and 69-bus~\cite{baran1989cap} radial
feeders with the MATPOWER data~\cite{zimmerman2011} (open tie lines removed).
Five aggregators connect at buses 6, 12, 18, 25 and 30 of the 33-bus feeder
(9, 21, 35, 49 and 61 on the 69-bus feeder), from electrically strong to weak
locations (Fig.~\ref{fig:feeder}). Each aggregator serves its vehicles through
a \SI{500}{kW} transformer. The substation voltage is held at $1.03\pu$ throughout. With
constant-power loads the radial AC power-flow equations are
\begin{equation}
\mathbf{V}=V_0\mathbf{1}-\mathbf{Z}^{\mathrm{path}}\,\overline{\left(\mathbf{S}\oslash\mathbf{V}\right)},
\label{eq:pf}
\end{equation}
where $\mathbf{S}$ is the complex load at the non-substation buses, $\oslash$
is element-wise division, the bar denotes complex conjugation, and
$Z^{\mathrm{path}}_{nm}$ is the impedance of the path shared by buses $n$ and
$m$ from the substation. We solve~\eqref{eq:pf} by the backward/forward
sweep~\cite{shirmohammadi1988} to $10^{-10}\pu$; our tests match
pandapower's Newton--Raphson solution~\cite{thurner2018} to $10^{-8}\pu$. A power
flow is solved every \SI{60}{s} of simulated time.

\begin{figure}[t]
\centering
\includegraphics[width=0.9\columnwidth]{generated/fig_feeder_ieee33.pdf}
\caption{IEEE 33-bus feeder (MATPOWER data, open ties removed) with the five
aggregator connection points.}
\label{fig:feeder}
\end{figure}

\subsection{Data}
\emph{Prices.} Hourly Netherlands day-ahead prices from the ENTSO-E
Transparency Platform~\cite{hirth2018}, as distributed with
EV2Gym~\cite{orfanoudakis2025ev2gym}, converted to local standard time:
2023 for training, 2024 for testing, and 2019 as an alternative price regime.

\emph{Household load.} One year of \SI{15}{min} consumption of 25 Pecan Street
homes~\cite{pecanstreet}, as distributed with EV2Gym~\cite{orfanoudakis2025ev2gym},
averaged and normalized by its 99.5th percentile. The profile scales the
nominal feeder loads, matched by day of year, with multiplicative noise of
standard deviation 0.02 at every power-flow step. The base-load scale is
calibrated as the largest value (to 0.01) for which the feeder \emph{without}
EVs stays at or above $0.955\pu$ over the whole year
(\GScaleIeeeThreeThree{} for the 33-bus and \GScaleIeeeSixNine{} for the 69-bus
feeder). The voltage problems studied here are therefore caused by EV charging.

\emph{Vehicles.} The main experiments use a synthetic residential fleet whose
parameters are stated assumptions: arrivals $\mathcal{N}(18,2^2)$\,h clipped to
12:00--23:30, dwell $\mathcal{N}(12,3^2)$\,h clipped to 2--16\,h, initial and
target state of charge $\mathcal{N}(0.35,0.15^2)$ and $\mathcal{N}(0.85,0.10^2)$,
batteries of 40--\SI{100}{kWh}, and \SI{11}{kW} chargers with efficiency
0.95. Episodes run 24\,h from 12:00. For generalization we also use real
sessions from ACN-Data~\cite{lee2019acn} at Caltech and JPL (bundled with
SustainGym~\cite{yeh2023sustaingym}): each sampled vehicle keeps a recorded
session's arrival time, dwell and delivered energy (2019 for training,
2020--2021 for testing, weekdays, episodes from 06:00). Requests are capped at
what the charger can deliver during the dwell, so full service is always
attainable. EV penetration is the number of vehicles per household, with 300
households behind the five aggregators.

\subsection{Driver response}
Each vehicle accepts the execution price $p_k$ of its aggregator with the
Fishbein--Ajzen attitude model~\cite{fishbein1975},
\begin{equation}
P^{\mathrm{acc}}_i=\sigma\!\left(w^{\mathrm{c}}_i\frac{\lambda^{\mathrm{ref}}-p_k}{\lambda^{\mathrm{ref}}}+w^{\mathrm{n}}_i\bar A+b_i\right),
\label{eq:fishbein}
\end{equation}
with logistic $\sigma$, reference rate $\lambda^{\mathrm{ref}}=\SI{0.20}{\text{\euro}/kWh}$,
last-interval fleet acceptance $\bar A$ (floored at 0.3) and heterogeneous
weights $w^{\mathrm{c}}_i\sim\mathcal{N}(5,1)$, $w^{\mathrm{n}}_i\sim\mathcal{N}(2,0.5^2)$,
$b_i\sim\mathcal{N}(0,0.5^2)$. A driver whose remaining need exceeds 0.7 of what
the charger can still deliver accepts regardless of price. Acceptance is drawn
once per dispatch interval. The model is stylized; Section~\ref{sec:discussion}
discusses this limitation.

\subsection{Energy accounting and metrics}
A vehicle draws power only while it is plugged in, has accepted the current
price and still needs energy, and never more than completes its need within a
step. The energy cost is the day-ahead price times the energy actually drawn
(after any curtailment). We report the daily cost (\euro), the cost per
delivered kWh, the service quality (SQ, delivered over requested energy), the
violation rate (share of \SI{60}{s} steps with any bus below
$0.95\pu$), the minimum voltage, the curtailed energy, and the mean retail
price paid by drivers.

\section{Nested Controller}
\label{sec:method}
Fig.~\ref{fig:arch} shows the architecture. Each level is a decision process
at its own rate whose environment includes the closed-loop behavior of the
faster levels: Level~1 acts every hour, Level~2 every \SI{15}{min}, Level~3a
every \SI{15}{min} and Level~3b every \SI{60}{s}. Set points flow down
(corridor $\rightarrow$ execution price and set point $\rightarrow$ per-vehicle
rates $\rightarrow$ reactive injections); measurements flow up (voltages, cost,
curtailment and acceptance enter the states and rewards of the levels above).

\begin{figure*}[t]
\centering
\includegraphics[width=0.92\textwidth]{generated/fig_architecture.pdf}
\caption{Nested controller. Set points flow down (blue), reactive set points
are computed locally (orange), and measurements flow back up (red, dashed).}
\label{fig:arch}
\end{figure*}

\subsection{Level 1: price corridor (PPO, hourly)}
The state $s^{(1)}_t\in\mathbb{R}^{11}$ holds the mean bus voltage, the
substation active and reactive power, the current day-ahead price, the share of
vehicles plugged in, their mean state of charge, the line-loading margin, the
substation loading, the hour (sine and cosine) and the mean price over the
next 12\,h. The action $a^{(1)}_t\in[0,1]^2$, drawn from Beta distributions,
sets the centre $c_t$ and width $w_t$ of the corridor
$[p^{\min}_t,p^{\max}_t]=[c_t-w_t/2,\,c_t+w_t/2]$ (clipped to
$[p^{\mathrm{lo}},p^{\mathrm{hi}}]$):
\begin{align}
c_t&=\lambda^{\mathrm{ref}}+(2a^{(1)}_{t,1}-1)\begin{cases}\lambda^{\mathrm{ref}}-p^{\mathrm{lo}}, & a^{(1)}_{t,1}<0.5,\\ p^{\mathrm{hi}}-\lambda^{\mathrm{ref}}, & \text{otherwise,}\end{cases}\nonumber\\
w_t&=w^{\min}+a^{(1)}_{t,2}\,(w^{\max}-w^{\min}),
\label{eq:corridor}
\end{align}
with bounds $p^{\mathrm{lo}}=0.05$, $p^{\mathrm{hi}}=\SI{0.40}{\text{\euro}/kWh}$ and
widths $w^{\min}=0.02$, $w^{\max}=0.20$. The neutral action $(0.5,0.5)$ centres
the corridor on the reference rate, so an untrained policy charges the flat
tariff of the baselines. The reward of hour $t$,
\begin{align}
r^{(1)}_t={}&-\frac{C_t}{100}-50\,(20\,\Delta V_t)^2-10\,\mathbb{1}[\Delta V_t>0]\nonumber\\
&-5\,\frac{U_t}{100}-0.5\,\frac{X_t}{100}+\omega\,\frac{R_t-\lambda^{\mathrm{ref}}E^{\mathrm{del}}_t}{100},
\label{eq:r1}
\end{align}
penalizes energy cost $C_t$, the voltage deficit $\Delta V_t=\max(0,\vmin-V^{\min}_t)$,
unmet energy $U_t$ of departing vehicles and curtailment $X_t$; the last term,
with retail revenue $R_t$ and delivered energy $E^{\mathrm{del}}_t$, is the
revenue-neutrality term defined below. PPO~\cite{schulman2017} trains the
policy with clipping 0.2, $\gamma=0.99$ and GAE $\lambda=0.95$.

\subsection{Level 2: plan-residual dispatch (DDPG, \SI{15}{min})}
\emph{State.} The state of aggregator $k$, $s^{(2)}_{\tau,k}\in\mathbb{R}^{28}$,
holds its bus voltage, the hour, the current price, the day-ahead prices of
the current and the next 11 hours, the corridor, the number of plugged-in vehicles, their
remaining energy need (total, and split into four laxity bins), the power they
can absorb, their mean remaining dwell, the last acceptance rate, and the plan
set point $u^0_{\tau,k}$ defined below. One actor--critic is shared by the five
aggregators, with a one-hot aggregator identifier appended to the state
(parameter sharing~\cite{gupta2017}).

\emph{Planning prior.} For each plugged-in vehicle $i$ with remaining need
$e_i$, the plan selects the $\lceil e_i/(\eta\bar c\Delta)\rceil$ cheapest
intervals before departure ($\bar c=\SI{11}{kW}$ charger rating, $\eta=0.95$,
$\Delta=\SI{15}{min}$); prices beyond the 12\,h look-ahead are
valued at the mean known price. The plan set point $u^0_{\tau,k}\in[0,1]$ is
the power of the vehicles whose current interval is selected, as a fraction of
the power the aggregator can deliver now. The plan needs only the information
already in the state.

\emph{Action.} The actor outputs $a_{\tau,k}\in[0,1]^2$. The first component
corrects the plan,
\begin{equation}
u_{\tau,k}=\mathrm{clip}\big(u^0_{\tau,k}+\rho\,(2a_{\tau,k,1}-1),\,0,\,1\big),
\label{eq:residual}
\end{equation}
so an actor output of $a=0.5$ reproduces the plan; the residual scale $\rho$ is
listed in Table~\ref{tab:hyper}. The second component sets the execution price inside the corridor,
$p_{\tau,k}=p^{\min}_t+a_{\tau,k,2}(p^{\max}_t-p^{\min}_t)$.

\emph{Feasibility by construction.} Let $\hat c_i=\min\{\bar c,\,e_i/(\eta\Delta)\}$
for the vehicles that accepted the price. The set point dispatches
$P_{\tau,k}=u_{\tau,k}\min\{P^{\mathrm{cap}}_k,\sum_i\hat c_i\}$, which is
filled in order of increasing laxity $\ell_i=h_i-e_i/(\eta\bar c)$ ($h_i$:
hours to departure)~\cite{xu2016priority}. A deadline guard raises $P_{\tau,k}$
to cover every vehicle with $\ell_i\le\Delta$. Every dispatch therefore lies in
\begin{equation}
\mathcal{C}_k=\Big\{c:\ 0\le c_i\le\hat c_i,\ \textstyle\sum_i c_i\le P^{\mathrm{cap}}_k\Big\}.
\label{eq:feasible}
\end{equation}
Methods that output per-vehicle rates are mapped onto $\mathcal{C}_k$ by exact
Euclidean projection (bisection on the dual of the sum constraint).

\emph{Reward.} The reward of aggregator $k$ in interval $\tau$ is
\begin{align}
r^{(2)}_{\tau,k}={}&-C_{\tau,k}+\omega\,(p_{\tau,k}-\lambda^{\mathrm{ref}})E^{\mathrm{del}}_{\tau,k}\nonumber\\
&-2\,U_{\tau,k}-0.5\,G_{\tau,k}-0.5\,X_{\tau,k},
\label{eq:r2}
\end{align}
where $C_{\tau,k}$ is the energy cost of the interval (summed over a day it is
exactly the daily cost), $U_{\tau,k}$ the unmet energy of departing vehicles,
$G_{\tau,k}$ the energy that can no longer be delivered before departure and
$X_{\tau,k}$ the curtailed energy (all in kWh, money in \euro). Because one day
spans 96 decisions, we use $\gamma=0.999$; with $\gamma=0.99$ a cost incurred
12\,h later, e.g.\ in the cheapest night hours seen from the afternoon, is
discounted by almost 40\% ($0.99^{48}\approx0.62$).

\emph{Revenue-neutral pricing.} A profit-seeking aggregator would raise retail
prices, which lowers acceptance and pushes charging into expensive hours. We
instead require the mean retail price paid to equal the flat reference rate
$\lambda^{\mathrm{ref}}$ charged by the non-pricing baselines. The weight
$\omega$ in~\eqref{eq:r1}--\eqref{eq:r2} is the Lagrange multiplier of this
constraint. Plain dual ascent oscillated in our experiments, so we use a PI
Lagrangian update~\cite{stooke2020pid} after every training episode,
\begin{align}
e&=(\lambda^{\mathrm{ref}}-\bar p)/\lambda^{\mathrm{ref}},\qquad \bar e\leftarrow(1-\alpha)\,\bar e+\alpha\,e,\nonumber\\
\omega&=\mathrm{clip}\Big(K_p\,\bar e+K_i\textstyle\sum e,\ \omega^{\min},\ \omega^{\max}\Big),
\label{eq:dual}
\end{align}
where $\bar p$ is the mean retail price paid in the episode and the integral
is clipped against wind-up (gains and bounds in Table~\ref{tab:hyper}). The
multiplier holds the \emph{training-time} average; the final deterministic
policy can still sit above or below it. After training we therefore calibrate
the tariff level: a constant offset added to every execution price is found by
bisection such that, on ten 2023 training days, the deterministic policy's mean
retail price paid equals $\lambda^{\mathrm{ref}}$. The same calibration is
applied to every learned method, and only training data are used. Prices can
thus shift charging in time while drivers pay about the reference rate; the
realized retail prices on the test days are reported with the results.

DDPG~\cite{lillicrap2016} trains the actor and critic (256--128--64 units) on
transitions $(s_\tau,a_\tau,r_\tau,s_{\tau+1})$, where $a_\tau$ is the action
\emph{actually applied} after the guard, mapped back
through~\eqref{eq:residual}. The actor's output layer is initialized near zero,
so training starts from the plan.

\subsection{Level 3: price acceptance and reactive correction}
Level~3a is the acceptance model~\eqref{eq:fishbein}. Level~3b runs inside
every \SI{60}{s} step (Fig.~\ref{fig:l3}). After the power flow, if
$\min_n V_n<\vmin+\delta$ (with $\vmin=0.95$ and $\delta=0.001\pu$), the
plugged-in chargers at aggregator bus $k$ offer the headroom
\begin{equation}
\bar Q_k=\sum_{i\in k}\sqrt{S_i^2-P_i^2},\qquad S_i=\SI{12}{kVA}.
\label{eq:qcap}
\end{equation}
A charger at $P_i=0$ thus offers its full rating, and curtailing active power
\emph{increases} reactive headroom. The first injection is proportional to
the voltage gap, weighted toward the most depressed buses. Each later
iteration measures the sensitivity $\hat\sigma=\Delta V^{\min}/\Delta Q$
between the last two power-flow solutions and injects
\begin{equation}
\Delta Q=1.2\,\big(\vmin+\delta-V^{\min}\big)/\hat\sigma,
\label{eq:newton}
\end{equation}
split across buses by voltage depression and capped by the remaining headroom.
If no headroom is left, EV power is shed in steps of up to 20\% per iteration,
most at the most depressed bus, and the flow is re-solved. The loop stops when
$V^{\min}\ge\vmin+\delta$, or after eight power flows; once curtailment has
started, up to twelve further power flows let it complete. Because the sensitivity
is measured on successive AC solutions, the step needs no precomputed network
model.
Level~3b does not depend on the policy above it; we therefore also evaluate
it under every baseline (``+L3'').

\begin{figure}[t]
\centering
\includegraphics[width=0.7\columnwidth]{generated/fig_l3_loop.pdf}
\caption{Level-3b correction inside one \SI{60}{s} step.}
\label{fig:l3}
\end{figure}

\subsection{Training}
Episodes are random 2023 days. A curriculum raises the fleet from 60 to 300
vehicles in steps of 60 and advances when the last 20 episodes reach mean
SQ $\ge0.95$ with mean curtailment $\le\SI{20}{kWh}$; the final stage draws
the fleet size uniformly from 120--300. Each run has
\GTrainEpisodes{} episodes. Algorithm~\ref{alg:main} summarizes one dispatch
interval, and Table~\ref{tab:hyper} lists the hyperparameters, read directly
from the configuration file.

\begin{algorithm}[t]
\caption{One \SI{15}{min} interval of the nested controller}
\label{alg:main}
\begin{algorithmic}[1]
\STATE \textbf{if} hour boundary \textbf{then} observe $s^{(1)}$; set corridor by~\eqref{eq:corridor}
\FOR{each aggregator $k$}
  \STATE observe $s^{(2)}_k$ (incl.\ plan $u^0_k$); $a_k\leftarrow\mu(s^{(2)}_k)$
  \STATE set point $u_k$ by~\eqref{eq:residual}; execution price $p_k$
\ENDFOR
\STATE drivers accept or decline by~\eqref{eq:fishbein}
\STATE LLF allocation with deadline guard onto $\mathcal{C}_k$~\eqref{eq:feasible}
\FOR{each of the fifteen \SI{60}{s} steps}
  \STATE solve the AC power flow~\eqref{eq:pf}
  \STATE \textbf{if} $V^{\min}<\vmin+\delta$ \textbf{then} Level-3b loop~\eqref{eq:qcap}--\eqref{eq:newton}
  \STATE book drawn energy, cost and curtailment
\ENDFOR
\STATE (training) store $(s,a^{\mathrm{applied}},r,s')$ and update the agents
\STATE (training, end of day) update the multiplier $\omega$ by~\eqref{eq:dual}
\end{algorithmic}
\end{algorithm}

\centering
\caption{Hyperparameters, read from the configuration file of the code.}
\label{tab:hyper}

\section{Experimental Setup}
\label{sec:setup}

\subsection{Scenarios}
S1, S2, S3 and S5 use 120, 200, 240 and 300 vehicles (40--100\% penetration).
S4 repeats S3 with a 15\% hourly-persistent base-load forecast
error. Two stress tests probe Level~3: S6 forbids all charging between 19:00
and 20:00 (a failure mode in which reactive capacity tied to charging power
would vanish), and S7 has 360 vehicles (120\%) with inverters derated to
50\%.

\subsection{Baselines}
\emph{Rules.} Uncoordinated charging (full power on arrival); a TOU timer
(off-peak 23:00--07:00, earlier only when laxity is exhausted); and the
price-aware heuristic, which charges each vehicle at full power in its planned
cheapest intervals, that is, the Level-2 plan executed per vehicle, with the
same 12\,h price look-ahead.
\emph{Model-predictive LP-OPF.} At every interval an LP over the rest of the
day (HiGHS~\cite{huangfu2018}) minimizes energy cost plus a
\SI{5}{\text{\euro}/kWh} penalty on unmet energy, subject to per-vehicle energy,
charger and transformer limits and to linearized voltage limits
($\ge\vmin+\delta$ at every bus) from finite-difference sensitivities of the
AC power flow at the forecast operating point. It has \emph{perfect
foresight} of prices and of every vehicle's arrival, departure and need. It is
a strong model-based reference rather than a deployable controller; it is not a
strict bound, because its voltage model is linearized and drivers may still
decline.
\emph{Learned.} Flat DDPG (one agent, all aggregators' states and actions),
PPO-Lagrangian and CPO~\cite{achiam2017} (expected-cost constraint on
violations, limit $d=0$), and a goal-conditioned hierarchical RL agent
(hourly DDPG goals, \SI{15}{min} DDPG workers). They observe the same states,
including the plan set point, use the same allocation layer, reward terms,
discount factor and revenue-neutral multiplier, and add a voltage penalty
because they are trained without Level~3. Each is also evaluated with Level~3
attached. Uncoordinated charging, the price-aware heuristic and the LP-OPF
charge the flat reference rate $\lambda^{\mathrm{ref}}$; the TOU timer charges
its three-tier tariff (0.12, 0.20 and \SI{0.30}{\text{\euro}/kWh} off-peak,
mid-peak and 17:00--21:00).

\subsection{Protocol}
All methods are evaluated on the same \GEvalDays{} distinct 2024 days, with
identical fleets and noise for each day (paired design). Learned methods are
trained with \GTrainSeeds{} seeds; each day's metric is averaged over seeds.
We report means with 95\% bootstrap confidence intervals over days (10\,000
resamples) and compare methods with Wilcoxon signed-rank tests on the paired
daily differences, Holm-corrected across the comparison family.
